young.html: For parents: this story, about big-game hunting, a troubled marriage and a fatal shot, is for adult readers. This path introduces Hemingway's famous way of writing instead.

Ernest Hemingway was an American writer who loved the outdoors: fishing, hunting, mountains and the sea. He was famous for writing short, plain sentences. He believed a good story is like an iceberg: you see only the tip above the water, but most of it is hidden underneath. A writer can leave things out, and readers will still feel them.

young.name: gb-hemingway-iceberg
young.cap: Hemingway's iceberg: tap each layer, from what is said down to what is only felt.

young.html: Write an iceberg. Write a short scene, five sentences, about two people at breakfast after an argument. Don't say what the argument was about, and don't name any feelings. Only describe what they do and say. Then read it to your family: can they guess what is under the surface?

full.html: Ernest Hemingway (1899–1961) grew up in Oak Park, Illinois, worked as a newspaper reporter, and was badly wounded as a Red Cross ambulance driver in Italy in 1918. In Paris in the 1920s he developed his spare, clipped style; The Sun Also Rises (1926) and A Farewell to Arms (1929) made him famous. A safari in East Africa in 1933–34 gave him the setting for this story, published in 1936. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954.
About quotations: the story was first published in 1936 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

It opens at lunch in a safari camp in East Africa. Everyone pretends nothing has happened, but something has: that morning, Francis Macomber, a wealthy American, ran in panic from a wounded, charging lion, and the professional hunter, Robert Wilson, had to kill it. Macomber's wife, Margot, makes no secret of her contempt, and her open scorn humiliates him further.

The story then goes back to tell the lion hunt in full, partly through Macomber's fear and even, for a moment, the lion's own view. The next day they hunt buffalo. In the heat of the chase, Macomber suddenly loses his fear and feels a wild happiness, as if he has become a man at last. Wilson is pleased; Margot is uneasy, because a brave husband will not be so easy to rule. When a wounded buffalo charges, Macomber stands his ground. Margot fires from the car, and her shot kills her husband.

full.name: gb-hemingway-iceberg
full.cap: What the story shows, and what it leaves under the surface: our summary.

full.html: Did she mean it? Hemingway never says. Wilson, cold and contemptuous, suggests that she did. Many readers take him at his word; others point out that she may have been aiming at the buffalo. The title is ironic and sincere at once: Macomber's "happy life," the life of a man without fear, lasted only minutes.
Hemingway's subject is courage: what it is, how it is lost and found, and what it costs. Wilson lives by a strict code of grace under pressure. Macomber, in the end, earns it.
His "iceberg" method, leaving the deepest feelings unsaid, makes readers do the work of understanding. The open ending is a result of that method.
Taking Wilson as the author's voice. He embodies the code Hemingway admired, but the story also shows his coldness, his own failings and his contempt for the Macombers.

items: Aristotle's Ethics, earlier on this ladder, defines courage as the right mean between cowardice and rashness; Macomber swings from one to the edge of the other.
Homer's Iliad shows warriors shamed by fear and restored by valor.
Conrad and Lawrence, earlier in this era, also test men in hard places far from home.
Hemingway's style shaped generations of American writers and journalists.
What is courage? Is it the absence of fear, or acting well while afraid?
Can one moment change who a person is?
Why might a writer leave the most important thing unsaid?
How should we treat someone who has failed in front of others?

questions: Have you ever been afraid and then found your courage? What helped?
Margot mocked her husband when he failed. How should we treat someone who is ashamed?
Why do you think Hemingway didn't tell us whether Margot meant to fire at her husband?
What do you think the title means?
Is it better to say exactly what you feel, or can leaving things unsaid be powerful?
care: Big-game hunting, a troubled marriage and a fatal shooting, told plainly; for adult readers. The lesson summarizes without detail.
